title: Halving Recursions and the Logarithm
quickIdea: Halve the argument and the depth is the number of bits; the value such a recursion returns is a logarithm.
remember: bar(n) = 0 at n = 1, else 1 + bar(n/2), returns floor(log2 n): the number of halvings needed to reach 1. bar(2) = 1, bar(4) = 2, bar(16) = 4, bar(65536) = 16.
Composing it - foo(n) = 1 + foo(bar(n)) with foo(1) = 1 - iterates the logarithm, so foo(n) counts how many times log2 can be applied before the value is 1.
GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.51 asks for the smallest n with foo(n) = 5. The chain is 65536, 16, 4, 2, 1: five activations, so the answer is 2^16 = 65536. foo(256) = 4 shows that nothing smaller works.
Halving recursions have depth Theta(log n), which is why binary search, exponentiation by squaring and Euclid's algorithm by division use a logarithmic number of frames.

The linear-depth twin is subtraction instead of division. GATE CSE 2021 Set 2 Q.23: SomeFunction(15, 255) subtracts until the arguments are equal and returns 15, using sixteen calls where division would use two.
Watch the floor: floor(log2 n) is the exponent of the largest power of two not exceeding n, so bar(3) = 1 and bar(7) = 2, not 2 and 3.

example.prompt: int bar(int n) { if (n == 1) return 0; return 1 + bar(n/2); } What is bar(65536), and what is the smallest n with bar(n) = 5?
example.work: 65536 -> 32768 -> ... -> 1 takes sixteen halvings, so bar(65536) = 16 = log2(65536). For bar(n) = 5 the smallest n is the smallest with floor(log2 n) = 5, that is 2^5 = 32.
example.answer: bar(65536) = 16, and the smallest n with bar(n) = 5 is 32.

gateAngle: 2026 Set 1 Q.51 is this card plus one composition: recognise floor(log2 n), then count how many applications are needed. Recognising the logarithm turns a search into one line of arithmetic.

variations.why: Repeated subtraction is Euclid's algorithm with linear depth; the answer is gcd(15, 255).

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For the same bar, what is the smallest n with bar(n) = 5, and how deep is the recursion for n = 1024?
variations.answer: n = 32; and 1024 gives bar(1024) = 10, so eleven frames are alive at the deepest point.
variations.why: The inverse direction of the 2026 question: from a value of the logarithm to the smallest argument.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a halving recursion cost O(log n) frames while a subtraction recursion for the same problem costs O(n)?
variations.answer: Because the argument shrinks geometrically in the first case and only linearly in the second. Depth is the number of steps to the base case, so it is the number of halvings against the number of subtractions.
variations.why: Explains why 2021 Q.23 needs sixteen calls and division-based gcd would need two.

trap.what: Assuming a halving recursion always reaches its base case.
trap.why: Halving has a fixed point at 0. A base case written as n == 1 is safe only for n >= 1; for n = 0 the argument never changes and the recursion never ends.
trap.counterexample: With bar as defined above, bar(0) calls bar(0) for ever, because 0 == 1 is false and 0/2 is 0.
